newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian government unveils new extradition law.
newsitem.headline: Colombian government unveils new extradition law.

text.p: Colombia's government asked Congress on Tuesday to lift a ban on extradition, a prohibition that President Ernesto Samper said had turned the country into a "sanctuary" for international criminals.

Legislation that would lift the ban was presented to the Senate by newly appointed Justice Minister Almabeatriz Rengifo, minutes after she was sworn in by Samper in a ceremony at the ornate Casa de Narino presidential palace.

"The time has come to set clearly, and by law, a policy of extradition," Samper said after giving the oath of office to Rengifo, a little known lawyer who served as his special legal counsellor until she was appointed last week.

Rengifo is the third justice minister to serve in Samper's 2 1/2-year-old government. She replaced Carlos Medellin, a top proponent of extradition who stepped down to work on the presidential campaign of Carlos Lleras de la Fuente.

By moving to restore extradition, Samper said the government hoped to end "the nightmare of drugs" that has tormented Colombia for nearly two decades. It would also prevent criminal drug syndicates from using Colombia as "a sanctuary for protection from punishment of the crimes they commit abroad," he said.
"The time has come for criminals, terrorists and drug traffickers to be warned that it offends us when they use Colombian justice as a shield of impunity for their crimes," Samper said.

Political analysts and diplomats say the government faces a long, uphill battle to win approval of the extradition law, since most Colombians oppose the practice and drug barons have demonstrated an uncanny ability to influence many legislators in the past.

Further clouding the outlook is the fact that constitutional reforms have to be approved by two consecutive sessions of Congress. The current session ends on June 20, leaving little time for it to be debated and approved for final ratification by the session beginning on July 20.

The ban on extradition was approved by the constituent assembly after years of violence that saw hundreds of people, including three presidential candidates, a justice minister, high court judges, journalists and scores of police killed in a campaign of assassinations and bombings that drug lords waged against extradition in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Referring to that period, which is still fresh in the minds of most Colombians, Samper said the country had stopped extraditing its criminals "by force of terrorism and threats."
U.S. officials have said repeatedly that detention in a secure prison facility in the United States is what Colombia's powerful drug lords fear the most.
